track.name: finance-prep
track.label: Finance & Business Operations Prep
track.summary: Everything a finance or operations role assumes on day one: accounting, the three statements, business math, corporate finance, how operations turn into numbers, and the tools to show your work.

phases.title: Accounting Foundations I: The Equation, Debits & Credits
phases.description: The accounting equation and double-entry bookkeeping, the language every other topic in this course builds on.

phases.title: Accounting Foundations II: The Accounting Cycle & Adjustments
phases.description: How transactions flow from journal to trial balance, and why accrual accounting needs adjusting entries.

phases.title: Accounting Foundations III: Inventory, Depreciation & Closing the Books
phases.description: How companies allocate the cost of inventory and long-lived assets over time, and how the books are closed at period end.

phases.title: Reading the Three Financial Statements
phases.description: Turning the bookkeeping mechanics of Phases 1-3 into fluent reading of an income statement, balance sheet and cash flow statement, and how the three connect.

phases.title: Reading a Real Annual Report
phases.description: Where the statements live inside an actual 10-K or annual report, and the narrative sections (MD&A, footnotes, auditor's report) around them.

phases.title: Business Math for Finance
phases.description: The arithmetic every finance role assumes: growth rates and compounding, plus enough statistics and probability to read a variance or a forecast confidently.

phases.title: Time Value of Money & Corporate Finance Math
phases.description: A dollar today is worth more than a dollar tomorrow: present and future value, annuities and perpetuities, and the NPV/IRR decision rules built on them.

phases.title: Corporate Finance Fundamentals
phases.description: How a company finances itself, what that financing costs, and how it decides which projects are worth funding.

phases.title: Economics for Business
phases.description: The supply/demand and market-structure vocabulary behind pricing decisions, plus enough macro (GDP, inflation, rates, FX) to read business news intelligently.

phases.title: Business & Revenue Models, Cost Behaviour & Break-Even
phases.description: How a business actually makes money, how its costs behave as volume changes, and the break-even math that ties the two together.

phases.title: Costing Methods & Unit Economics
phases.description: How a company assigns cost to what it makes -- by job, by process, or by activity -- and how it boils a whole business down to the economics of one customer or unit.

phases.title: Working Capital, Cash & Supply Chain Basics
phases.description: How cash gets tied up in day-to-day operations -- inventory, receivables, payables -- and the basics of managing physical supply chains that drive those numbers.

phases.title: Budgeting Basics & Management Reporting
phases.description: How a company plans its year in numbers, and how it reports on itself internally once actual results come in.

phases.title: Entity Types, Business Law & Tax Basics
phases.description: The legal and tax shape a business takes -- sole proprietorship, LLC, corporation -- and the handful of tax and contract basics every finance role bumps into.

phases.title: Excel, PowerPoint & Business Writing for Finance
phases.description: The minimum tool fluency to show your work: enough Excel to build the models above, enough PowerPoint to present them, and enough business writing to explain them in a sentence.

topics.title: The Accounting Equation & Double-Entry Bookkeeping
topics.description: Assets = Liabilities + Equity is the identity every transaction must preserve. Understanding why keeps every later statement and model sane.

steps.d: State Assets = Liabilities + Equity for a sole proprietorship, and the equity/net-assets variants for a corporation and a nonprofit.
Pick five simple transactions (cash sale, loan, purchase on credit, owner investment, expense paid) and show how each keeps the equation balanced.

steps.t: Read the OpenStax chapter on the equation
steps.d: Read the relevant chapter of the free OpenStax accounting textbook and note how it defines an account.
Score yourself on the accounting-equation quiz and redo any transaction type you got wrong.

topics.title: Debits, Credits, Journal Entries & T-Accounts
topics.description: Debits and credits are just the mechanics for keeping the equation balanced. This topic drills the rules until they are automatic.

steps.t: Memorize the five account types' normal balances
steps.d: Write out whether assets, liabilities, equity, revenue and expenses normally carry debit or credit balances.
Write journal entries for ten varied transactions, labelling each debit and credit.
Post your ten journal entries into T-accounts and total each one.
Watch the Farber Academy T-accounts video and compare its method to yours.
Retake the AccountingCoach debits-and-credits quiz until you can do it without hesitating.

topics.title: The Accounting Cycle & Trial Balance
topics.description: The repeatable sequence -- journalize, post, trial balance, adjust, report, close -- that produces a company's books every period.

steps.t: List the cycle's steps in order
steps.d: Write out the accounting cycle from identifying a transaction through the post-closing trial balance.
From a small set of T-accounts, list every account and balance into a trial balance and confirm debits equal credits.
Deliberately introduce one error (a transposed number or a missed entry) and describe how you would find it from an unbalanced trial balance.

steps.t: Compare a manual cycle to software
steps.d: Read how the same steps happen instantly inside accounting software today versus a manual ledger.

topics.title: Accruals, Deferrals & Adjusting Entries
topics.description: Why the books need adjusting before statements can be trusted: expenses and revenues that straddle period boundaries.

steps.d: State, in your own words, when you'd use an accrual adjusting entry versus a deferral adjusting entry.
Journalize the December accrual for a plumbing bill received in January, as in the AccountingCoach example.
Journalize splitting a six-month prepaid insurance payment across two accounting periods.
Create your own examples of accrued revenue, accrued expense, deferred revenue and deferred expense, and journalize each.

topics.title: Revenue Recognition Basics (Accrual Accounting)
topics.description: The rule that revenue is recorded when earned, not when cash arrives -- the foundation later revenue-recognition standards build on.

steps.d: Write the rule: revenue is recorded when earned/delivered, matched against when cash may arrive separately.
Work through cash-at-sale, bill-now-pay-later, and pay-in-advance scenarios and identify which account is debited alongside the revenue credit each time.
Watch the Khan Academy video comparing accrual and cash accounting and note one case where they'd report different profit for the same month.

topics.title: Inventory Costing Methods (FIFO, LIFO, Weighted Average)
topics.description: The cost-flow assumption a company chooses changes reported profit and inventory value even when nothing physical changes.

steps.t: Build one inventory ledger, three ways
steps.d: Take one sequence of purchases and one sale quantity, and compute COGS and ending inventory under FIFO, LIFO and weighted average.
In your own words, explain why LIFO produces lower gross profit than FIFO when costs are rising.

steps.t: Identify which method fits which business
steps.d: Note which method suits perishable goods versus commodities, and why.
Check your understanding of cost-flow assumptions with the self-graded quiz.

topics.title: Depreciation & Amortization
topics.description: How the cost of long-lived tangible and intangible assets is spread across the periods that benefit from them.

steps.d: Take a cost, salvage value and useful life and compute annual straight-line depreciation.
Recompute the same asset's depreciation using usage (e.g. machine hours) instead of time.
State which kinds of assets are amortized versus depreciated, and why the distinction matters for a patent versus a machine.

steps.t: Explain the choice to a manager
steps.d: Write two sentences explaining why a company might prefer straight-line versus an activity-based method for a given asset.

topics.title: Closing Entries & Preparing the Financial Statements
topics.description: The final step of the cycle: zeroing out temporary accounts into retained earnings so next period starts clean, and producing the statements.

steps.d: Identify which accounts are temporary (closed each period) versus permanent (carried forward).
From a small trial balance with revenue and expense accounts, write the closing entries into retained earnings.
List the balances that remain after closing and confirm only balance-sheet accounts appear.
Trace how the closed net income figure flows into the equity section of the balance sheet.

topics.title: The Income Statement
topics.description: Revenue down to net income, and the operating/non-operating distinctions that matter for interpretation.

steps.d: Take a public company's income statement and label revenue, COGS, gross profit, operating expenses, operating income and net income.
Watch the income-statement introduction video and note anything it defines differently than you expected.
Complete the Khan Academy 'Interpreting the Income Statement' practice exercises.

topics.title: The Balance Sheet
topics.description: Assets, liabilities and equity at a point in time, and how current vs. non-current items are ordered.

steps.d: Take a public company's balance sheet and group each line into current assets, non-current assets, current liabilities, non-current liabilities and equity.
Add up each side and confirm assets equal liabilities plus equity.
Complete the Khan Academy 'Interpreting the Balance Sheet' practice exercises.

topics.title: The Cash Flow Statement & Statement Linkages
topics.description: Why net income isn't cash, how the cash flow statement reconciles the two, and how all three statements tie together.

steps.t: Watch the basic cash flow statement video
steps.d: Watch Khan Academy's cash flow statement video and note the three sections: operating, investing, financing.

steps.t: Trace one number across all three statements
steps.d: Pick net income from the income statement and trace where it appears (or is adjusted) in the cash flow statement and equity section of the balance sheet.

steps.t: Read the AccountingCoach financial statements explanation
steps.d: Read the full explanation covering all three statements together and how they're presented.
Watch this short video and write one sentence connecting retained earnings to net income.

topics.title: 10-K Structure & Finding Filings on EDGAR
topics.description: Where a real 10-K lives, its standard parts (Business, Risk Factors, MD&A, Financial Statements), and how to pull one up yourself.

steps.d: Read the SEC/Investor.gov guide on how to read a 10-K and note its list of key sections.

steps.t: Open EDGAR and find a filing
steps.d: Use SEC EDGAR's company search to find and open a real company's most recent 10-K.
Inside that 10-K, locate the Business, Risk Factors, MD&A and Financial Statements sections and note their item numbers.
Note from the SEC bulletin how a quarterly 10-Q differs from the annual 10-K in scope and detail.

topics.title: MD&A, Footnotes & the Auditor's Report
topics.description: The narrative and disclosure layers around the numbers: management's own explanation, the fine print, and the independent check on it all.

steps.d: Read the SEC's Beginners' Guide to Financial Statements for its framing of what each statement and disclosure is for.
In the 10-K you opened last topic, read the MD&A and summarize its view of the year's performance in three sentences.
Open the notes to the financial statements in the same filing and identify the first note (accounting policies) and one other note that surprises you.
Locate the independent auditor's report in the filing and identify which opinion it gives (unqualified/clean, or otherwise).

topics.title: Growth Rates, Percentages & Compounding
topics.description: Percentage growth and compounding show up in every model that follows -- revenue growth, interest, inflation, returns.

steps.d: Given a starting and ending value across one period, compute the percentage growth by hand.
Watch the Khan Academy video and apply the same method to three of your own numbers.
Read Khan Academy's compound-growth article and contrast simple growth compounded once versus compounded across several periods.
Given a beginning and ending value over several years, compute the compound annual growth rate using the CAGR formula.

topics.title: Basic Statistics & Probability for Finance
topics.description: Mean, variance, standard deviation and basic probability -- the vocabulary behind risk, forecasting error and 'expected value.'

steps.t: Compute mean and standard deviation by hand
steps.d: Take a small data set (e.g. six months of sales) and compute its mean and standard deviation.
Read Khan Academy's article on the idea of spread and standard deviation, and restate in your own words what a bigger standard deviation means.
Work through Seeing Theory's basic probability and compound probability visualizations.
Solve one expected-value word problem (e.g. an insurance or a bet) using the probabilities and payoffs you're given.

topics.title: Present Value & Future Value
topics.description: The core idea that money now is worth more than the same amount later, and the discounting math that quantifies it.

steps.t: Watch the Khan Academy time value of money video
steps.d: Watch the video and write the present-value formula PV = FV / (1+r)^n from memory afterward.
Given a present amount, a rate and a number of periods, compute the future value by hand.
Given a future amount, a rate and a number of periods, compute the present value by hand.
Watch the follow-up Khan Academy videos and note how the discount rate changes the present value.

topics.title: Annuities & Perpetuities
topics.description: Valuing a stream of equal payments, whether it ends after a fixed number of periods (annuity) or continues forever (perpetuity).

steps.d: Read the Wall Street Prep annuity page and work through its present-value-of-an-annuity example by hand.
Given a fixed annual payment and a discount rate, compute PV = C / r.
Given a first-year payment, a discount rate and a growth rate, compute PV = C / (r - g) and note why r must exceed g.

steps.t: Apply it to a real case
steps.d: Value a hypothetical preferred stock paying a fixed annual dividend as a perpetuity.

topics.title: NPV & IRR: The Capital Budgeting Decision Rules
topics.description: How a company decides whether a project is worth doing: discount every cash flow back to today (NPV) or solve for the rate that makes NPV zero (IRR).

steps.t: Watch present value 4 and discounted cash flow
steps.d: Watch the Khan Academy video connecting present value to a full discounted cash flow.
Given an initial outlay and three years of cash flows, discount each and sum to a net present value.

steps.t: Read the MIT OCW capital budgeting materials
steps.d: Read/skim the MIT Finance Theory I capital budgeting lecture and note its stated limitations of IRR versus NPV.

steps.t: Explain the NPV vs IRR conflict
steps.d: Write two sentences on why NPV and IRR can disagree in ranking two mutually exclusive projects, and which rule wins.

topics.title: Debt vs. Equity Financing
topics.description: The two basic ways a company raises money, and the different claims and risks each gives investors.

steps.t: Watch the equity vs debt video
steps.d: Watch Khan Academy's equity vs. debt video and write one sentence on what each investor type is owed.
Note three differences between debt and equity financing (repayment obligation, tax treatment, control/ownership).
Classify a bond, a share of common stock and a bank loan as debt or equity and justify each.

topics.title: Cost of Capital: Cost of Debt, Cost of Equity & WACC
topics.description: The blended rate a company must earn to satisfy everyone who has financed it -- the discount rate behind every NPV calculation.

steps.d: Given a company's interest rate on debt and its tax rate, compute the after-tax cost of debt.

steps.t: Compute a cost of equity with CAPM
steps.d: Given a risk-free rate, a beta and a market risk premium, compute the cost of equity using Ke = Rf + beta x ERP.
Given the market values of debt and equity, weight the two costs into a single WACC.
Read through a full worked WACC example and compare its structure to your own calculation.

topics.title: Capital Budgeting Basics: Payback Period & Choosing Among Rules
topics.description: The simplest capital budgeting rule (how fast do we get our money back?) and why it's used alongside, not instead of, NPV and IRR.

steps.d: Given an initial outlay and a series of annual cash inflows, compute how many years it takes to recover the investment.
State why payback period ignores the time value of money and cash flows after the payback point.

steps.t: Read the capital budgeting methods chapter
steps.d: Read the OER chapter comparing payback, NPV and IRR and note when a company might still use payback despite its flaws.
Given three hypothetical projects' cash flows, rank them by payback period, then by NPV, and note if the rankings differ.

topics.title: Supply, Demand & Market Structures
topics.description: How price and quantity settle at equilibrium, and how that changes depending on how competitive the market is.

steps.d: Sketch a market and show what happens to equilibrium price and quantity when demand increases.
Watch the Khan Academy video and check your sketch against its worked example.
List perfect competition, monopolistic competition, oligopoly and monopoly in order of pricing power, with one real example of each.

steps.t: Explain why it matters for a business
steps.d: Write two sentences on how a company's pricing strategy would differ if it operated in a perfectly competitive market versus a monopoly.

topics.title: Macro Indicators: GDP, Inflation & Interest Rates
topics.description: The handful of numbers -- GDP, CPI/inflation, interest rates -- that every business plan and forecast has to sit inside.

steps.d: Watch the value-added or income/expenditure approach to GDP and note which approach makes more intuitive sense to you.
Watch or read the limitations-of-GDP material and list two things GDP doesn't capture.
Given a nominal rate and inflation rate, compute the approximate real interest rate.
Watch Khan Academy's inflation overview video and write one sentence on who is helped and who is hurt by unexpected inflation.

topics.title: Foreign Exchange (FX) Basics
topics.description: How currencies are priced against each other and why FX rates matter to any business that buys, sells or borrows across borders.

steps.d: Watch Khan Academy's video and write down, in your own words, what it means for a currency to 'strengthen' against another.
Given an exchange rate, convert a price from one currency to another and back.

steps.t: Explain the impact on an exporter
steps.d: State how a stronger home currency affects a domestic exporter's competitiveness abroad.
Complete Khan Academy's foreign exchange market practice exercise.

topics.title: Business & Revenue Models
topics.description: How a company decides what it sells, to whom, and how it gets paid -- subscription, transaction, service, affiliate and more.

steps.d: Name five distinct revenue models (e.g. subscription, transaction, service, affiliate, freemium) and one company that uses each.

steps.t: Read the CMU revenue models note
steps.d: Read the Swartz Center for Entrepreneurship's revenue models overview and note which model best fits a business you know.

steps.t: Map a business model canvas, lightly
steps.d: For one real company, write one sentence each on who its customer is, what it sells them, and how it gets paid.

steps.t: Explain the business-model vs revenue-model distinction
steps.d: State in one sentence how a 'business model' (the whole value-creation story) differs from a 'revenue model' (just how money comes in).

topics.title: Cost Behaviour: Fixed, Variable & Break-Even
topics.description: Which costs move with volume and which don't, and the point at which revenue finally covers them all.

steps.d: Take ten costs from a hypothetical small business (rent, materials, hourly labor, insurance, etc.) and classify each as fixed or variable.
Watch Khan Academy's video and check your classifications against its definitions.
Given fixed costs, price per unit and variable cost per unit, compute the break-even quantity using Fixed Costs / (Price - Variable Cost).

steps.t: Re-run it after a cost change
steps.d: Increase the variable cost per unit and recompute break-even, noting which direction it moves and why.

topics.title: Contribution Margin, CVP & Pricing Basics
topics.description: Contribution margin drives cost-volume-profit analysis and pricing decisions -- how much of each extra sale actually reaches profit.

steps.t: Compute contribution margin, in dollars and percent
steps.d: Given a selling price and variable cost per unit, compute the contribution margin per unit and the contribution margin ratio.
Given a target profit figure, compute the sales volume needed using the same contribution-margin logic as break-even.
Watch Khan Academy's video and compute one elasticity value using the midpoint method.
State whether a company facing inelastic demand should raise or lower price to increase revenue, and why.

topics.title: Job Order Costing & Process Costing
topics.description: Two ways to track manufacturing cost: per unique job (a custom order) or per continuous process (mass production).

steps.d: Read the job-order-costing and process-costing pages and write one sentence defining each.
For five different businesses (construction firm, soda bottler, consulting firm, furniture batch-maker, oil refinery), decide which costing method fits and why.

steps.t: Read the Lumen 'Jobs v. Processes' chapter
steps.d: Read the chapter and note the structural difference in how Work in Process inventory accounts are set up under each method.

topics.title: Activity-Based Costing (ABC)
topics.description: A more precise way to assign overhead: trace cost to the activities that actually drive it, then to the products that use those activities.

steps.d: Read the full explanation and note the difference between a traditional overhead allocation and an activity-based one.
For a manufacturer, name three activities (e.g. machine setups, special testing, engineering changes) that could each be their own ABC cost pool.

steps.t: Explain why low-volume products cost more under ABC
steps.d: State why a low-volume, highly customized product often gets assigned more overhead under ABC than under a simple machine-hours allocation.
Check your understanding with the AccountingCoach activity-based-costing quiz.

topics.title: Unit Economics for a Business
topics.description: Boiling a whole business down to the profitability of one customer or one unit sold -- the lens investors and operators both use to judge whether growth is healthy.

steps.d: Write one-sentence definitions of customer acquisition cost and customer lifetime value.

steps.t: Read the Visible.vc unit economics guide
steps.d: Read the guide and note the LTV:CAC ratio it flags as a healthy benchmark.

steps.t: Read the a16z startup metrics piece
steps.d: Skim the a16z article and list three metrics beyond CAC/LTV that it says investors look at.

steps.t: Compute a simple unit economics case
steps.d: Given a CAC, an average revenue per customer per month, a gross margin and a churn rate, estimate whether the LTV:CAC ratio is healthy.

topics.title: Working Capital & the Cash Conversion Cycle
topics.description: Current assets minus current liabilities, and the cycle that shows how many days cash is tied up between paying suppliers and collecting from customers.

steps.d: Given a list of current assets and current liabilities, compute working capital and say whether it's healthy.
From the same numbers, compute the current ratio and the quick ratio, and explain why the quick ratio excludes inventory.
Given days inventory outstanding, days sales outstanding and days payable outstanding, compute CCC = DIO + DSO - DPO.
Name one lever a company could pull on each of DIO, DSO and DPO to shorten its cash conversion cycle.

topics.title: Inventory & Supply Chain Fundamentals
topics.description: The tradeoff between ordering too often (higher ordering cost) and ordering too much (higher holding cost) that sits behind every inventory decision.

steps.d: Given annual demand, order cost per order and holding cost per unit, compute the economic order quantity using EOQ = sqrt(2DS/H).
State in your own words why a bigger order quantity lowers ordering cost but raises holding cost.

steps.t: Skim the MIT OCW supply chain course
steps.d: Skim the MIT logistics and supply chain management lecture notes and note one topic (e.g. risk pooling, multi-echelon planning) beyond basic EOQ.
For a product you use, sketch its supply chain from raw material to your hands, in five steps or fewer.

topics.title: Budgeting Basics & the Master Budget
topics.description: What a budget is for, and how individual budgets (sales, labor, materials) roll up into one master budget for the year.

steps.t: Read what a budget is for
steps.d: Read AccountingCoach's explanation of budgeting and note its stated purpose beyond just 'predicting the future.'
Read the Lumen Learning chapter and list which lower-level budgets typically roll up into a master budget.
For a small hypothetical business, sketch a one-page budget with revenue, a few cost lines, and a bottom-line profit projection.

topics.title: Management Reporting & Variance Basics
topics.description: How internal reports differ from external financial statements, and the basic mechanics of comparing actual results to budget.

steps.d: Read AccountingCoach's explanation and note two ways internal reports can look different from GAAP financial statements.
Given a budgeted and an actual figure for one cost line, compute the variance and label it favorable or unfavorable.
Read the Lumen Learning chapter on budget variances and note what 'management by exception' means.

steps.t: Explain a flexible budget in one sentence
steps.d: State why a flexible budget adjusts for actual volume before comparing costs, rather than comparing against the original fixed budget.

topics.title: Business Entity Types & Contract Basics
topics.description: How a business is legally organized changes who's liable, how it's taxed, and what a contract with it can bind.

steps.d: Read the SBA's page comparing sole proprietorship, LLC and corporation, and note the liability and tax difference for each.

steps.t: Pick a structure for a hypothetical business
steps.d: For a small hypothetical consulting business, decide which entity type you'd recommend and justify it in two sentences.

steps.t: Read the Cornell LII contracts overview
steps.d: Read the Wex contracts category page and note the definition of a legally binding contract and which contracts must be in writing.

topics.title: Tax Basics for a Business
topics.description: The handful of tax types (income, self-employment, employment) a business owner or finance employee needs to recognize, even without doing the filing.

steps.t: List the general business tax types
steps.d: Read the IRS business-taxes page and list income tax, self-employment tax and employment tax with one sentence on who owes each.
State how an LLC's pass-through taxation differs from a C-corporation's, including the double-taxation point for corporate dividends.

steps.t: Skim the small business tax guide
steps.d: Skim IRS Publication 334 and note one recordkeeping requirement that surprises you.

topics.title: Excel Quick-Start for Finance
topics.description: Just enough Excel -- SUM, AVERAGE, IF, a lookup function -- to build the small models used throughout this course. Dedicated Excel tracks go far deeper than this.

steps.d: Enter a small data set and compute totals and averages with SUM and AVERAGE.
Write a formula that labels each row 'over budget' or 'on budget' based on a comparison.
Use VLOOKUP or XLOOKUP to pull a matching value from a second table.
Skim ExcelJet's formula reference and bookmark three functions you expect to need again in this course.

topics.title: PowerPoint Basics for Presenting Numbers
topics.description: Enough PowerPoint mechanics to turn an analysis into a handful of clear slides.

steps.d: Following Microsoft's basic-tasks guide, create a title slide plus three content slides on any small topic.
Apply one consistent theme and use appropriate slide layouts for a title, a bulleted list, and a chart or table slide.
Insert one simple chart or table summarizing a small data set, and title it in one clear sentence.

topics.title: Business Writing for Numbers
topics.description: Turning an analysis into a short, clear written summary a busy reader can act on.

steps.t: Read the Purdue OWL clarity page
steps.d: Read the page on revising for clarity and rewrite one wordy sentence from your own recent work more concisely.
Read Purdue OWL's page on prioritizing concerns in business writing and note what it says should come first in a business message.
Take any analysis you've done in this course and summarize it in exactly three sentences a manager could act on.
